articles.title: America built a fortress after 9/11. Then the threat started hiding in plain sight
articles.summary: Twenty-five years after 9/11, lone actors radicalized online have replaced al Qaeda's complex plots as the greatest terrorism threat to the homeland.
articles.body: On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, Javed Ali drove past the Pentagon on his way to work in northern Virginia. Roughly half an hour later, American Airlines Flight 77 slammed into the building. From his office in Falls Church, Ali could see smoke rising from the Pentagon. A year later, in a turn that captured how dramatically the country had changed, he was walking into the still-damaged building himself — now working in the Defense Intelligence Agency's counterterrorism office. TRUMP CONFIRMS PENTAGON PLANS FOR 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 ATTACKS, DISPUTES REPORT ON GROUND ZERO ABSENCE "It was a very eerie and odd and surreal moment in my career," Ali told Fox News Digital. Ali's career would eventually take him from the DIA to the newly created Department of Homeland Security and later the FBI, giving him a front-row seat to the enormous national security architecture America constructed after the deadliest foreign attack on U.S. soil. Twenty-five years later, that architecture presents something of a paradox. By one of its clearest measures, the post-9/11 system appears to have made another attack on the scale of 9/11 far harder. The United States has not suffered another terrorist attack remotely approaching the scale and complexity of 9/11, which killed 2,977 people. U.S. intelligence and military operations dismantled much of the al Qaeda network that planned it, while new agencies, surveillance authorities, watchlists and intelligence-sharing systems were designed to ensure that another group could not exploit the same seams in American defenses. The 2026 U.S. intelligence community assessment said counterterrorism operations have degraded al Qaeda and ISIS's ability to quickly rebuild their leadership and plan large-scale attacks against the U.S. homeland. But success against the threat of 2001 did not eliminate terrorism. It helped change it. AMERICAN YOUTH RADICALIZED ONLINE, BUSTED IN SUSPECTED TERROR PLOTS AFTER HATING COUNTRY ON SOCIAL MEDIA Today's most difficult threats increasingly involve individuals radicalized online, small cells with little warning signature, foreign terrorist organizations seeking to inspire attacks from afar, and an expanding layer of cyber and state-sponsored threats capable of reaching deep inside the United States without hijacking an airplane. The question 25 years after 9/11, therefore, is not simply whether Americans are safer. They are safer from one kind of attack — while increasingly exposed to others. AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY Building a security state after 9/11 The scale of the American response was extraordinary. Just over two months after the attacks, President George W. Bush signed legislation creating the Transportation Security Administration. TSA says its creation amounted to the largest civilian undertaking in U.S. government history at the time, with the federal government rapidly assuming responsibility for airport passenger and baggage screening. The following year, Congress created the Department of Homeland Security, combining all or part of 22 federal agencies and offices. DHS began operating in March 2003 and today employs more than 260,000 people across missions ranging from border and aviation security to cybersecurity, intelligence and emergency response. The changes went far beyond new agencies. The 9/11 Commission found that the pre-attack breakdown was deeper than the familiar failure to "connect the dots." Responsibility had been scattered across agencies, information was not consistently shared, and no single entity was empowered to integrate intelligence and drive joint action across the foreign-domestic divide. The commission concluded that "responsibility and accountability were diffuse." Washington spent the next two decades trying to close those gaps. Brown University's Costs of War project estimates that post-9/11 wars and related obligations have cost roughly $8 trillion. It estimates that more than $1.1 trillion has been spent on homeland security efforts to prevent and counterterrorism inside the United States since DHS was created. Al Qaeda didn't disappear overnight Ali said it can be easy, with 25 years of hindsight, to forget how persistent the original threat remained. Even after the United States invaded Afghanistan, killed or captured senior al Qaeda figures and put the organization under extraordinary pressure, the group continued attempting to find ways back into the homeland. During Ali's years at DHS, he said officials repeatedly confronted plots involving al Qaeda and its affiliates, including a 2006 plot originating in Britain to bomb transatlantic airliners traveling to North America. The threat then evolved again. Usama bin Laden was killed by U.S. forces in Pakistan in May 2011. But rather than marking the end of the era of jihadist terrorism, the following years produced a new and in some ways more difficult challenge. ISIS grew out of al Qaeda in Iraq, expanded rapidly amid the wars in Iraq and Syria and declared a self-described caliphate in June 2014. At its height, the group controlled vast territory and millions of people in Iraq and Syria while encouraging or directing attacks far beyond its borders. The State Department reported that ISIS had emerged from al Qaeda in Iraq and expanded dramatically during 2013 and 2014. For U.S. counterterrorism officials, Ali said, the center of gravity increasingly shifted from identifying trained operatives sent by an organized group to finding individuals who might be radicalizing inside Western countries. Then came another shift: attacks by lone offenders across different ideologies, often with no direct operational relationship to an organization overseas. "Mostly lone actors, lone offenders, not tied to groups overseas, not traveling overseas, and not being directed by people overseas," said Ali, now an associate professor of practice at the University of Michigan's Ford School of Public Policy. DHS CHIEF ANNOUNCES CHANGES TO ITS SEAL TO REFLECT THAT DEPARTMENT IS 'AT WAR EVERY SINGLE DAY' The terrorist organization became a phone screen The transformation is now reflected in the government's own threat assessments. The 2026 Annual Threat Assessment from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence said setbacks to the ability of Islamist terrorist groups to conduct "large-scale complex attacks" have pushed them toward information operations and propaganda designed to inspire or enable people in or with access to Western countries. The assessment said there were at least three Islamist terrorist attacks in the United States in 2025 and that law enforcement disrupted at least 15 U.S.-based Islamist terrorist plotters that year. Roughly half of those disrupted plotters had some online contact with Islamist terrorists or were inspired by foreign terrorist organizations, according to the assessment. The vulnerability was demonstrated on New Year's Day 2025, when Shamsud-Din Jabbar, a U.S. citizen from Texas, drove a pickup truck into a crowd on Bourbon Street in New Orleans, killing 14 people. The FBI described the attack as an act of terrorism and said Jabbar had become increasingly isolated before adopting extremist views. In the days after that attack, the FBI said lone actors and small cells who radicalize online had posed the greatest terrorism threat to the homeland in recent years precisely because they can be so difficult to detect and disrupt. That presents almost the inverse of the 9/11 problem. The 9/11 plot required 19 hijackers, overseas leadership, financing, international travel, flight training and years of planning. The challenge for investigators was collecting pieces of information held across different agencies and assembling them quickly enough. A lone actor may offer far fewer pieces to collect in the first place. Ali said many recent attackers or alleged plotters had not previously come onto the radar of the FBI or local law enforcement, leaving authorities with the extraordinarily difficult task of identifying people who may not commit an obvious crime until they move toward violence. "So yes, we are safer from a certain type of threat," Ali said, "but again, we are not immune from terrorism, and other types of threats are much more difficult to identify or stop." KASH PATEL REVEALS THE CHILLING HOLIDAY TERROR PLOTS FBI FEDERAL AGENTS QUIETLY STOPPED A security system built for yesterday? That changing threat has also fueled a broader debate over whether the institutions created after 9/11 became too large, too expensive or too focused on the dangers of the previous era. Morgan Murphy, who served as press secretary to the secretary of Defense during the first Trump administration and later worked in the Trump White House, argues that Washington built too much bureaucracy around the 9/11 threat while other vulnerabilities grew. "TSA agents still pat down grandma and gum up travel while Beijing wires our living rooms with cheap TVs and selfie sticks through the supply chain handed to them by Clinton, Bush, Obama and Biden," Murphy said. "We spent two decades frisking American passengers while our adversaries plugged themselves into our homes and businesses." "The genius of America after Pearl Harbor was that we built to fight. After 9/11, we built to process," Murphy told Fox News Digital, "Real security means sovereignty at home and lethality abroad — a sealed border, an untangled supply chain, and enemies who fear us." Theo Wold, who served as acting assistant attorney general in the Justice Department's Office of Legal Policy and as deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy during the first Trump administration, offered a similar critique, arguing that post-9/11 Washington relied too heavily on large bureaucracies, expansive government authorities and wars in the Middle East. "George W. Bush and the D.C. governing elite responded to 9/11 the way their politics demanded: create large, unwieldy bureaucracy, push for special legal authorities with limited oversight and activate ground wars in the Middle East," Wold told Fox News Digital. "Those wars didn’t make us safer, the legal authorities were wielded against Americans, and the bureaucracy is full of waste and has proven nearly unworkable," he said. Wold argued that the lesson from the past quarter-century should be a more narrowly targeted national-security model. "Now we know better. Americans are safest when we are nimble and focus ruthlessly on targeting real enemies," he said. The next threat may not look like 9/11 The challenge now extends beyond terrorism. The 2026 intelligence assessment warns that China, Russia, Iran, North Korea and non-state ransomware groups continue seeking access to U.S. government networks and private critical infrastructure for espionage, financial gain and possible future disruption. It also warns that artificial intelligence is accelerating cyber capabilities and that several state adversaries are developing missile systems capable of threatening the homeland. The security landscape that began with al Qaeda operatives training to fly passenger jets has therefore expanded into something far less geographically defined: terrorist propaganda transmitted to an individual's phone, malicious code inserted into a computer network, attacks on critical infrastructure and state adversaries capable of reaching Americans from thousands of miles away. For Ali, however, the evolution of the threat should not lead Washington to conclude that the original threat has vanished. One of the central lessons of the years before Sept. 11, he said, was that emerging terrorist organizations have to be confronted before they have the time and space to develop operational capability. "When these terrorist threats start to emerge, whether it's overseas or here, you have to put pressure on them before they gather momentum to carry out operations," Ali said. The danger, he argued, would be allowing counterterrorism to fall so far down Washington's list of priorities that the country begins recreating the complacency that existed before 9/11. "Terrorism as a tactic is probably never going to be defeated," Ali said. Twenty-five years after he watched smoke rise from the Pentagon, Ali's answer to whether America is safer reflects the contradiction at the heart of the post-9/11 era. The United States built a massive system to prevent the next 9/11. It appears to have made another 9/11 far harder to execute. articles.title: Saudi Arabia tells Trump now is the time for military action as Iran-backed Houthis advance
articles.summary: Houthi forces seized Perim island and key positions along Yemen's Bab al-Mandab Strait as Saudi Arabia urged Trump to take direct military action.
articles.body: Saudi Arabia is urging Washington to take direct military action against Iran-backed Houthis, Fox News Digital learned after the terrorist group seized key positions along Yemen’s Bab al-Mandab Strait on Friday. The dramatic strengthening of Houthi's positioning along the coastline of Yemen is in one of the world's most important shipping choke points — a narrow passage that links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, which has been used as a bypass as the Iran war continues to severely disrupt shipping, especially of oil, through the Strait of Hormuz. The rapid advance on Friday triggered urgent discussions at the highest levels in Riyadh and Washington, and a source familiar with the matter tells Fox News Digital that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman urged President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis. NEW RISK FOR U.S. CONSUMERS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS THREATEN A SECOND MAJOR OIL CHOKEPOINT The Houthis reached the strategic island of Mayyun, also known as Perim, after Yemeni government forces withdrew and also took the mainland coastal town of Dhubab, four Yemeni government sources told Reuters on Friday. Fox News Digital independently confirmed key elements of an Axios report with a source familiar with the matter, who said the crown prince spoke with Trump a few times over the past 24 hours about the escalating situation in Yemen. The U.S. does not want to take direct military action for now, but Trump told bin Salman that Washington would assist Saudi Arabia with intelligence and targeting support, according to the source. The source also confirmed that U.S. Central Command commander Adm. Brad Cooper traveled to Saudi Arabia for coordination talks. The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment on the calls or whether additional U.S. military action is under consideration. IRAN'S BIGGEST WEAPON AGAINST THE U.S. MAY BE SLIPPING AWAY, EXPERTS SAY The convergence raises the prospect of simultaneous pressure on two of the world’s most consequential maritime arteries: Iran disrupting traffic through Hormuz while its Houthi allies strengthen their position around Bab al-Mandab. Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that the shift reflects Tehran’s effort to recover leverage as pressure around Hormuz changes. "Trump’s success in pushing back on Iran’s maritime threat in the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf has made the regime lose the maritime leverage it had, and now it is looking to double down on the Houthis who have proven to be able to impact Red Sea shipping and the Bab al-Mandab Strait in the past," Ben Taleblu said. "As Tehran loses leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, it is trying to wield a knife and a handshake at once: diplomacy with Arab states and a knife in the back via the Houthi offensive," he added. IRAN CALLS ON HOUTHIS TO PREPARE TO CUT OFF RED SEA GATEWAY — CAN THE TERROR GROUP DO IT? The latest advance follows the Houthis’ capture Thursday of the strategic Red Sea port of Mocha, which was previously held by forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government. Former U.S. special envoy for Yemen Timothy Lenderking said Friday that the Houthis had spent the years since the 2022 U.N.-brokered truce rebuilding their military strength and are now exploiting the broader Iran conflict to increase pressure on Saudi Arabia. Speaking during an on-the-record Middle East Institute virtual briefing, Lenderking said the April 2022 truce largely put Yemen’s civil war on pause but also "did allow the Houthis to regroup, retrain, refit, restock." "They’re extremely entrepreneurial. They use every opportunity to build their capability, to test their capabilities, such that they are now the most lethal non-state actor in the entire Middle East," Lenderking said. Lenderking traced the latest round of escalation in part to Iranian Mahan Air flights into Sanaa earlier this summer, which he said brought personnel and equipment intended to support the Houthi war effort, adding that the personnel were from Iran and were "probably IRGC members." IRAN-BACKED HOUTHI THREAT IN RED SEA COULD LEAD TO MAJOR U.S. POLICY SHIFT, ANALYSTS SAY Lenderking said the Houthis are now taking advantage of the wider conflict with Iran to increase their leverage over Riyadh. "They’ve seized this opportunity, bringing these various lines of effort together, to put a great deal of pressure on the Yemen government and the Saudis specifically," he said. On Thursday, a senior Trump administration official told Fox News Digital: "The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges. We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability." The stakes extend well beyond Yemen. The Bab al-Mandab is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point and serves as the southern gateway to the Suez Canal. About 7% of global oil output passed through the strait in June, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters. Disruption can force ships to reroute around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope, adding significant time and cost to voyages. Reuters reported Friday that only seven vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, compared with a prewar daily average of 125, underscoring the pressure already facing the region’s other critical maritime choke point. EXPERT WARNS OF 'GENERAL ESCALATION' OF FIGHTING IF HOUTHIS RESUME RED SEA CAMPAIGN Ben Taleblu said the speed of the Houthi advance exposed vulnerabilities in the Saudi-led effort to contain the group. "The U.S. should help the Saudis stymie the Houthi advance," he said. "The inability of the Saudis to prevent the Houthis from taking the strategic port city of Mocha, for example, does not bode well for what may come." Hisham Al-Omeisy, senior Yemen adviser at the European Institute of Peace, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that the danger extends beyond the territory captured. Retreating government forces, he said, left behind military equipment that could strengthen the Houthis on other fronts. "People are focused on taking Mocha and those outposts on the Red Sea," Al-Omeisy said. "But the military side is terrible, particularly the equipment, the munitions, the vehicles, the drones that were at those military camps, which they can now, in turn, use against the government forces elsewhere." articles.title: 'We will never, ever forget': Trump commemorates 25th anniversary of 9/11 terrorist attacks
articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks on Friday by remembering the nearly 3,000 people killed in the deadl.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks on Friday by remembering the nearly 3,000 people killed in the deadliest terror attack on US soil and linking the tragedy to his administration’s ongoing confrontation with Iran.Speaking at the Pentagon, where American Airlines Flight 77 crashed on September 11, 2001, Trump said the attacks had strengthened American resolve and paid tribute to the victims, first responders and service members.“We will never, ever forget,” Trump said. “That’s why we fight today. We don’t have a choice.” "For anyone who lived it, no words can do justice to the anguish of that day," he added.Further continuing his tribute, the US president said, "We cannot forget that moment of immense and horrible evil that took place in this world, bent on the destruction of all that is good. But this morning, we also remember how America responded to that wickedness. On days like 9/11, we learn what a country is truly made of."Trump also used the anniversary to defend the US war against Iran, saying American service members were working to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons. “We salute our first responders and law enforcement, and we love them,” Trump said. “And we salute the service members working right now to ensure the world's number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon.”Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also connected the September 11 attacks with the current conflict, saying the US military had “laid waste to the world’s most prolific state sponsor of terrorism” in its war against Iran.“Our warriors have fought an Islamic theocracy that has wished us death for nearly half a century, that cheered on 9/11, a regime that has sponsored terrorist attacks against Americans for decades, killing thousands, including our comrades in Iraq, in Afghanistan,” Hegseth said.9/11 anniversary: Victims remembered across USAt the Pentagon, Trump and first lady Melania Trump listened as the names of all 184 people killed in the attack on the building were read aloud, with a bell tolling between each name.Trump also recalled individual victims, including a woman who was pregnant with her first child, a family of four travelling to Australia and three sixth-graders on a field trip.In New York, families of victims gathered at Ground Zero in Lower Manhattan alongside Vice President JD Vance and four former US presidents. The ceremony began at 8:46 a.m. ET, the moment American Airlines Flight 11 struck the World Trade Center’s North Tower.Family members then read the names of all 2,977 people killed in the September 11 attacks, along with the six people who died in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing. Some of those reading the names this year were children who had never met the relatives they lost in the attacks.For the first time, a seventh moment of silence was observed for the thousands of people who have died since 2001 from illnesses linked to the toxic dust released after the attacks.At the Shanksville crash site in Pennsylvania, mourners remembered the 40 passengers and crew of United Airlines Flight 93, who died after passengers fought back against the hijackers and the plane crashed before reaching its intended target in Washington.The attacks led to the US invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq and the broader “war on terror”. They also contributed to a rise in anti-Muslim sentiment and hate crimes against Muslim Americans and immigrants from Muslim-majority countries.The human toll also continued long after September 11. Rescue workers, firefighters, police officers and others who spent weeks or months at Ground Zero were exposed to toxic substances in the air.The New York City Fire Department lost 343 members on September 11. More than 600 additional firefighters, including retired members involved in the rescue effort, have since died from 9/11-related illnesses, according to department figures.At Friday’s New York ceremony, the personal loss remained at the centre of the commemoration. Caroline Ogonowski, whose father John was the captain of Flight 11, brought her newborn son to his grandfather’s grave this year.“My father will never know his grandson. And my son will never know his grandfather,” she said.“We owe it to my father and all the others that we lost on that day to make sure that we continue to teach future generations about what happened, about who these people were, who these heroes were, how our country came together and became stronger because of it,” she added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: Europe News: Russian jet-powered drone attacks on Kyiv petrol stations killed two people and injured 12 on Friday, as Moscow and Kyiv exchanged fresh strikes on ci.
articles.body: Russian jet-powered drone attacks on Kyiv petrol stations killed two people and injured 12 on Friday, as Moscow and Kyiv exchanged fresh strikes on civilian and economic infrastructure.The attacks came amid an intensifying aerial campaign, with both sides reporting strikes on energy, logistics and other critical infrastructure as the war continues with little movement on the frontline.The attacks came a day after what appeared to be the first Russian strike on a petrol station in Kyiv. Russia has carried out almost daily attacks with faster jet-powered drones across the capital for the past two weeks, according to the report.“Russia's escalation with jet-powered 'shaheds' is gradually becoming increasingly terrorist in nature,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on X.Zelenskiy said Russia had also struck a building used by Ukraine's largest mobile operator, Kyivstar, in Kyiv, while attacks were reported in eight other Ukrainian regions. The company said its network continued to operate.A further eight people were injured in a separate overnight attack on a residential block in Kyiv, while a woman was killed in the wider Kyiv region, according to local officials.Bohdan Kukura, CEO of Ukrainian oil company Ukrnafta, said there was no military justification for the petrol station attacks.“There is no military objective behind such strikes. This is terror of the civilian population,” he said.Ukraine also launched drone attacks on Russian territory. Dmitry Milyayev, governor of the Tula region, said two people were killed and three injured in overnight strikes. Russia's Kursk governor said a 37-year-old man was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on Friday.Russian online retailer Ozon said a drone attack caused a fire at its logistics hub in Saratov. Ukraine's military said it had struck a Russian oil refinery in the region.The latest exchanges come as fighting along the front line has largely stalled more than four and a half years into the war. Both sides have increasingly targeted logistics, energy and other economic infrastructure in an effort to disrupt the other's war effort.Separately, Zelensky said on Thursday that there would be no trilateral meeting on ending the war before Russia's parliamentary elections on September 20. articles.title: Cardiff reacts to Fury vs Joshua at Principality Stadium rumours
articles.summary: As rumours of the fight grow, so too does the excitement among the city’s bars and restaurants.
articles.body:
"Bring it on, we are ready and waiting."

Those are the words of one Cardiff bar manager as rumours grow that the Principality Stadium could be the new front-runner to host Anthony Joshua's clash with Tyson Fury.

BBC Sport understands the Cardiff venue is being considered as an alternative to New York's Madison Square Garden and Wembley Stadium, sparking excitement among the Welsh capital's bars and restaurants.

City Arms manager Mark Falzon said: "It will be really exciting for us – we'll take some good money."

Similarly, Ffreya Davies, manager at Bar 44, said Joshua's previous fight at the Principality was a "huge day for us as a business", attracting "customers from all over the world".

For the richest fight in British boxing history to be held in Cardiff, Wales' nationwide 22:30 BST event curfew will need to be lifted to allow the 02:00 start time wanted by broadcasters Netflix.

The Principality Stadium's retractable roof means it could host the bout in late November despite colder and wetter weather, which could stand in the city's favour despite London Mayor Sadiq Khan's call for promoters to "get the fight to London".

Falzon, whose pub opposite the Principality, has a licence until 04:00, and said the fight would be a huge boost for the city.

"It's the biggest UK fight for the last 20 years," he said.

"Everyone will want to watch Fury and Joshua, whether they like boxing or not."

The pub would remove furniture, serve food and increase security if the fight goes ahead.

Falzon said: "The Oasis weekend [the band played two gigs in Cardiff in 2025] was the best atmosphere we've ever had in the city centre. If it matches that, it will be special.

Tapas bar manager Davies, meanwhile, said she would hope the business could catch the crowds before the fight.

"The footfall from stadium events is always great, but having two such huge names fighting just over the road would be amazing for business."

She said major events were "not only incredible for us as a business, but it's also just great to be able to show off Cardiff".

"It just brings people from all over the world," she said.

"There's something about having an event that the world is watching, happening just over the road, which is really quite special."

Her only concern was for residents living in nearby flats, although she said if the stadium's roof would be closed it could limit disruption late at night.

Nick Newman, chair of Cardiff Night Forum and manager of nine pubs in the city, said hosting the event would be "massive" news for Cardiff.

"We forecast the whole year in terms of activities, but obviously some events come at us unexpectedly," he said.

"It's almost a case of why wouldn't they bring it to Cardiff? We've got the best stadium in the world, with the best hospitality to go with it."

On concerns about licensing rules, Newman said the Licensing Act allowed organisers to apply for temporary event notices.

"I'm pretty sure the council would grant those, blanket grant them so to speak, because of the scale of the event. Obviously, we want to look after all the customers and tourists who come for it."

Paying tribute to the Swifties who flocked to Cardiff for Taylor Swift's shows, Newman said he believed this event could be "a slightly bigger scale, if that's possible" - even compared with Oasis.

He said visitors typically arrived several days early, providing a "massive boost" to the local economy.

"There's so many variables that we have to contend with.

"So anything that puts extra money in the tills means more hours for staff, which is all to the good.

"And for the local economy, again, it's just massive."

The location of the fights has been a major obstacle, with Fury casting doubt over whether it would even go ahead as recently as last month.

He had even suggested he would need to look for a new opponent after claiming Joshua was backing out of the fight.

Joshua's contract with Sela, the Saudi state-owned promotional company which is financing the showdown, stipulates it must take place in the UK.

When Sela turned their attention to New York with a 20 November date in order to capture a bigger audience for Netflix, Matchroom promoter Eddie Hearn demanded Joshua's purse be increased to reflect the additional tax paid for boxing in the United States.

Fury's agreement with Sela, meanwhile, is for the US, and he has repeatedly used social media to taunt Joshua over his reluctance to commit to anywhere other than the UK.

"It's inching closer and it looks like it could be the British boxing bonanza that we all hoped for taking place in Britain," Fury's manager Spencer Brown told Sky Sports.

"Three venues are still under consideration with Cardiff and Wembley still in the running."

articles.title: Helicopter engine fault behind Royal Navy serviceman's death
articles.summary: An investigation examined the causes of Lt Rhodri Leyshon's death during a helicopter exercise.
articles.body:
A helicopter engine fault was one factor behind the death of a Royal Navy serviceman during a training exercise, an investigation has concluded.

On 4 September 2024, three crew members were on board the Merlin Mk4, based at Royal Naval Air Station (RNAS) Yeovilton in Somerset, for night-flying exercises .

At about 20:50 GMT the aircraft ditched - a deliberate emergency landing on water, approximately 25 nautical miles south of Lyme Regis , Dorset.

A service inquiry found the right-hand seat pilot, Lt Rhodri Leyshon, had been "seriously injured" during the impact.

It also said he was "unable to escape from the aircraft as it entered the water".

The inquiry found the helicopter crashed after a diaphragm inside the engine split.

"This allowed fuel to flow through the diaphragm and into the engine," the inquiry report said.

"The excess fuel caused the engine to operate at a much faster speed than normal."

It said the crew members then "erroneously concluded that the number one and three engines had failed".

The report said these two engines were manually switched off, causing the remaining engine to reach its "overspeed trip threshold" and also deactivate.

"The loss of power from all three engines caused the aircraft to descend into the sea," it said.

Leyshon was recovered about two hours after the ditching and was pronounced dead in hospital, while the other two crew members suffered minor injuries.

The sunken helicopter had been "damaged beyond repair" and was recovered from the seabed in two major sections on 12 and 23 September 2024.

Air Marshal Alan Gillespie, who serves as the director general of the Defence Safety Authority, urged all commands to consider the 44 recommendations made by the service inquiry panel.

"On behalf of the Defence Safety Authority and the wider Defence Aviation community, I offer my sincere condolences to Lt Leyshon's family, friends and colleagues," he added.

articles.title: AfD win in Saxony-Anhalt leaves LGBT rights 'under threat,' says group
articles.summary: Following the resounding victory for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt, the Federation Queer Diversity in Germany (LSVD+) has warn...
articles.body:
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, leading to concerns from the Federation Queer Diversity in Germany (LSVD+) about the potential threats to LGBT rights and other marginalized groups.

The LSVD+ organization warned that the social climate in Saxony-Anhalt has already changed noticeably, with misanthropic views becoming more openly supported, leading to increased denial and hatred towards queer people, individuals who have experienced racism, those with a migrant background, and people with disabilities.

The LSVD+ is advocating for solidarity within democratic civil society to defend human rights, promote diversity, and protect individuals from exclusion, threats, and persecution in the face of the AfD's election victory.

Following the resounding victory for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt, the Federation Queer Diversity in Germany (LSVD+) has warned that queer people and other marginalized groups are set to face consequences.

"Our hard-won human rights for LGBTIQ* people are already not only constantly being called into question, but are also under active threat," said Alva Träbert from the Berlin-based organization on Friday.

LGBTIQ* stands for lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex, asexual and queer, with the asterisk serving as a placeholder for all other queer identities.

The AfD won 43.8% of the vote in Sunday's election and seeking to form a government despite narrowly missing out on a majority in the state parliament.

The LSVD+ said people from Saxony-Anhalt have already reported a distinctly noticeable change in the social climate.

"Misanthropic views have not only become more acceptable; they have long been openly and unashamedly supported," Träbert said.

Many queer people, people who have experienced racism, those with a migrant background or those with disabilities are facing increasing denial and open hatred in their everyday lives - and not just in Saxony-Anhalt, Träbert added.

"It is not just since Sunday that we have been asking ourselves: where and how can we safely be ourselves without exclusion, threats or persecution?"

The association is calling for solidarity within democratic civil society.

"It is up to all of us to shape and defend a diverse, democratic society, to look out for one another, and to stand up for our rights and those of our fellow human beings."

articles.title: At 17, British apprentice Tom Lear began building a 12.5-sq-m tiny home on a trailer from reclaimed materials; by 20, he owned it debt-free after spending just £6,000
articles.summary: UK News: A 20-year-old carpenter from Bristol has achieved debt-free homeownership after spending three years building a bespoke 12.5-square-metre mobile home .
articles.body: A 20-year-old carpenter from Bristol has achieved debt-free homeownership after spending three years building a bespoke 12.5-square-metre mobile home using reclaimed materials and timber offcuts. Tom Lear started the self-build project at the age of 17 while working as a carpentry apprentice on a low training wage. Working with a tight budget, Lear built the entire home on a donated flatbed trailer, keeping his total spending to about £6,000. The finished micro-home is 5 metres long, 2.4 metres wide and 4.5 metres high. It has a working kitchen, living area and mezzanine sleeping loft, along with insulation designed to make it suitable for living in throughout the year in the British climate. According to information compiled in the Frome Area Community Land Trust resource pack and reports by design publication Trend Hunter, Lear's project offers a possible alternative for young people who cannot afford traditional homes. By collecting unwanted materials from local building sites and using basic hand tools, Lear avoided the need for a commercial property loan, rent payments or a mortgage.Low apprenticeship wages sparked alternative housing planLear came up with the idea of building his own mobile home because of financial pressure during his early training years in Bristol. With rents high across the region, a large part of his apprentice income would have gone towards accommodation. Realising that buying a conventional home was out of reach on an apprentice wage, Lear looked to the growing tiny-home movement for ideas. “While I was on apprenticeship wage, I had no choice but to use reclaimed materials,” Lear explained in project documentation compiled by housing organisations. Instead of purchasing new timber and fittings, he collected unwanted materials from building sites, reclamation yards and local donors across Somerset and Bristol. Friends, family and local tradespeople also helped by providing materials. These included a heavy-duty twin-axle trailer that became the permanent base for the home. Over 36 months, Lear spent his evenings and weekends designing, building and finishing the timber-clad structure.Smart design makes the small space practicalAlthough the home has a footprint of only 12.5 square metres, its layout includes separate areas for cooking, living and sleeping while maintaining insulation and structural strength. The ground floor contains a small kitchen with reclaimed timber worktops, a sink and storage cabinets made from offcuts. Next to it is a compact living area with built-in seating and a small wood-burning stove that provides the main source of heat during winter. A fixed ladder leads to a raised mezzanine sleeping area with a full-sized double bed. The 4.5-metre height of the structure provides enough space for the loft. Windows recovered from renovation projects were positioned around the home to bring in natural light and help with passive solar heating. The cabin was also designed to meet UK towing rules on the maximum width and weight of mobile trailers, allowing it to remain road legal and potentially be moved in the future. Heavy insulation in the walls and roof helps reduce the amount of energy needed to heat the home, keeping daily running costs low compared with those of a standard house.Reclaimed materials cut construction costsThe project's costs show how reusing materials can reduce the expense of building a home. The trailer was the biggest individual cost because it provided the strong base needed to move the structure. The remaining £6,000 was spent on items such as specialist fasteners, roofing membranes, electrical components and safety equipment that could not be found second-hand. The exterior has treated timber cladding recovered from local site clearances. This protects the frame from moisture and decay. Inside, Lear used sanded pallet wood and discarded floorboards collected over three years. In coverage of the project by international lifestyle magazine Marie France, housing analysts said self-built homes using reclaimed materials could offer an alternative as deposit requirements continue to rise for first-time buyers in the UK. For Lear, finishing the project gave him both greater independence and a permanent home built almost entirely through his own labour.Growing interest in low-cost mobile homesLear's project reflects wider interest in small and mobile homes across the UK, as high land prices and mortgage costs make traditional homeownership difficult for many people. Community housing organisations, including the Frome Area Community Land Trust, have highlighted the project in educational resources as an example of low-cost and sustainable self-building. However, planning rules and access to land can make it difficult for people to keep tiny homes on wheels in urban areas for long periods. In rural areas, landowners and smallholders are increasingly considering mobile cabins for seasonal workers and affordable housing. After completing his tiny home debt-free at 20, Lear now has a fully mobile house that can be moved to different locations as his work needs change. The project also offers an example of how reclaimed materials and self-building can provide a lower-cost route to homeownership.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Mirwaiz to attend Iranian president's event in New Delhi
articles.summary: India News: SRINAGAR: Hurriyat Conference chairman Mirwaiz Umar Farooq left for New Delhi on Friday to attend an interaction with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshk.
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Hurriyat Conference chairman Mirwaiz Umar Farooq left for New Delhi on Friday to attend an interaction with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.In a statement issued here, Mirwaiz said following the invitation of the Iranian ambassador to India, he will be attending an interaction with President Pezeshkian, who is in the capital to attend the BRICS Summit.“The interaction of religious leaders, intellectuals and other dignitaries, is being hosted by Iran’s ambassador to India, Dr Mohammad Fathali, which is scheduled to take place in New Delhi later Friday followed by a dinner reception,” the statement said.In March this year, Mirwaiz, Kashmir’s chief cleric, had led a delegation of Kashmiri religious leaders to meet Dr Fathali at the Iranian embassy in New Delhi, where they expressed condolences over the killing of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, his family members and others and expressed “deep solidarity with the people of Iran.During the meeting, Mirwaiz had highlighted the “deep-rooted cultural, historical and religious ties between Kashmir and Iran,” stating that Kashmir has long been referred to as “Iran-e-Sagheer” (little Iran).After the killing of Khamenei, thousands of people in Kashmir gathered in Srinagar’s Lal Chowk and later in Budgam, with crowds stretching several kilometres, to mourn his death. The Valley also witnessed a large-scale donation drive following an appeal by the Iranian embassy, with people contributing cash, gold and even household items, vehicles and livestock.Former CM Mehbooba Mufti was the first political figure from J&K to visit the Iranian embassy to express solidarity.Later, on March 10, NC president Dr Farooq Abdullah visited the embassy and signed the condolence book on the “martyrdom of Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.”Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Did anyone go to jail in Kerala?’ Cong hits back at Omar amid Vande Mataram row
articles.summary: India News: SRINAGAR: A day after chief minister Omar Abdullah hit out at Congress for its criticism over full rendition of Vande Mataram and wondered if the part.
articles.body: SRINAGAR: A day after chief minister Omar Abdullah hit out at Congress for its criticism over full rendition of Vande Mataram and wondered if the party wanted Kashmiris to be arrested, J&K Congress president Tariq Hamid Karra sharpened the attack on ally NC, describing Omar’s comment as “detached from reality and highly unfortunate”.“The public has nothing to do with this debate. It is the govt that is expected to stand upright,” Karra said Friday in a statement. “Did a single person in Kerala go to jail when its govt chose to sing only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram at the Independence Day parade?” he asked.Karra also questioned if Omar was “capable of standing up for secular and inclusive values like the CMs of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Telangana had done by limiting Vande Mataram singing to first two stanzas at state events?”Earlier in the day, J&K deputy CM Surinder Choudhary had also dismissed Congress’s criticism, saying “Vande Mataram is our national song and we are proud of it”.On Thursday, Omar had said singing of the national song was a statutory and constitutional obligation, while responding to Congress’s objection to full rendition of Vande Mataram at the inaugural ceremony of the International Film Festival of Jammu & Kashmir. “All six stanzas of the national song must be played across the country at the govt events,” he said.Pointing out that legal action could be taken against those who failed to stand during the entire national song, Omar questioned whether Congress wanted more Kashmiris to be jailed.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Elon Musk reacts to Irish man's discovery that he would have to wait for 14 years to get Indian citizenship
articles.summary: US News: Aidan Joyce, a social media account that claimed to be an Irish man, said he fell in love with India and wanted to make Kolkata his home. He asked Elo.
articles.body: Aidan Joyce, a social media account that claimed to be an Irish man, said he fell in love with India and wanted to make Kolkata his home. He asked Elon Musk's AI chatbot Grok how he could move to the country permanently. The exchange caught the attention of Elon Musk, who reacted to the discussion on X with a brief assessment of India's immigration system: “India is realistic.”The Irish man, who had apparently been visiting Kolkata with his family, asked Grok about the possibility of becoming an Indian citizen. He wanted to know how quickly he could settle in the country and eventually obtain citizenship.Grok's response, however, made clear that moving to India permanently would not be an easy or quick process.According to the exchange shared online, the man was told that obtaining Indian citizenship could take at least 14 years, depending on his circumstances and the route he takes. He would first need to establish legal residence in India and meet the requirements for naturalisation.The answer also pointed out that India generally does not allow dual citizenship, meaning someone who becomes an Indian citizen would have to give up their existing citizenship."Wow that's a long time. Look, here is the story, I arrived with my partner and 2 children. Can we get some social welfare while we try and get a job. I'm totally skint at the moment, so I need a few $$ fast. How much will the Indian state pay us while we wait. Tell me briefly please," Joyce asked Grok. "None. India has no cash social welfare or unemployment payments for new arrivals or non-citizens. Ration cards, pensions and most assistance require Indian citizenship plus eligibility (e.g. BPL status). Formal-sector schemes need prior contributions. Support yourselves," the chatbot replied.Then Joyce asked if he could quickly buy a house in India and the answer was 'no'.What was the social media post all aboutThe post was meant to be a reality check for Indians who have been in the waiting line for Green Cards for years. It also showed that India does not offer any welfare and while visa holders can buy houses in the US, it is not so easy in India. But what started as a mockery turned into Elon Musk's endorsement for the Indian system."Hilarious thread of Irish guy asking about moving to India. It takes 12 years for citizenship, you must renounce previous passports, of course zero welfare -- they'll just deport you," one commented. Musk said India's system is realistic.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: USS Cole commander recalls chilling 9/11 warning at CIA just 20 minutes before first plane hit
articles.summary: Kirk Lippold warned CIA officials that a catastrophic attack was coming just 20 minutes before the first plane struck the World Trade Center.
articles.body: Just 20 minutes before the first hijacked plane struck the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001, the USS Cole's former commander made a chilling prediction inside CIA headquarters. Speaking on the "Fox News Rundown" podcast commemorating the 25th anniversary of 9/11, retired Navy Commander Kirk Lippold said the moment at Langley underscores a lesson he believes the nation cannot afford to forget. Lippold said he had just finished a briefing with a senior CIA official about intelligence related to the USS Cole attack. When asked for his assessment, Lippold warned that it would likely take a catastrophic event on U.S. soil for the American people to recognize the threat. FOR 'HORRIBLE MOMENT,' BUSH WHITE HOUSE THOUGHT US MILITARY SHOT DOWN FLIGHT 93 "I said, 'I'm [going to] be honest with you, sir. America doesn't understand. I believe it is going to take a seminal event probably in this country where hundreds, if not thousands, died before Americans realized that we are at war with this guy,' meaning [Osama] bin Laden," Lippold told Fox News' Lucas Tomlinson. "Twenty minutes after I said that, the first plane hit the North Tower, and I was literally leaving the headquarters when the plane hit the South Tower." 25 YEARS LATER, 9/11 MEMORIES ENDURE AS NATION GATHERS TO HONOR NEARLY 3,000 LIVES LOST The 9/11 terror attacks killed nearly 3,000 people, and thousands more have died from related illnesses. Less than a year before that day, Lippold was the commanding officer of the USS Cole when al Qaeda terrorists attacked the guided-missile destroyer. On Oct. 12, 2000, two suicide bombers in a small boat pulled alongside the ship in Aden, Yemen, offering friendly gestures before detonating explosives in their boat alongside the Cole. Seventeen U.S. sailors were killed, and 37 others were injured in the blast, which ripped a hole near the ship's waterline. AMERICA BUILT A FORTRESS AFTER 9/11; THEN THE THREAT STARTED HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT That incident was one of several al Qaeda attacks in the years leading up to 9/11, including the 1998 U.S. embassy bombings in East Africa, when Lippold argues went largely unanswered by U.S. leadership. For Lippold, watching the Pentagon burn on 9/11 reinforced his belief that the United States must aggressively confront terrorist groups around the globe. "It really solidified to me the costs that if the United States does not react to the threat of terrorism and countries who support it, we will continue to pay a price in the future," Lippold said. 9/11 WIDOW TERRY STRADA ACCUSES US OF PROTECTING SAUDI ARABIA 25 YEARS AFTER TERROR ATTACKS, ADDRESSES VANCE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "And it really doesn't matter whether it is through the drugs, whether it's through actually [an] attack, through waterborne or vehicle-borne improvised explosive devices, terrorism has to be ruthlessly stopped anywhere around the world," he added.

articles.title: In 2025, Connecticut student Vihaan Kamath started selling homemade cookies for charity; by August 2026, his nonprofit had raised $66,331 and helped nearly 1,000 children
articles.summary: US News: A Connecticut teenager has turned his love of baking into a growing nonprofit that has raised more than $66,000 to support children in need.Vihaan Kam.
articles.body: A Connecticut teenager has turned his love of baking into a growing nonprofit that has raised more than $66,000 to support children in need.Vihaan Kamath, 16, a Greenwich-area high school student preparing to enter his senior year, founded Cookie for a Cause in April 2025. The nonprofit sells homemade cookies and directs its proceeds toward children’s charities, including St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital and Yale New Haven Children’s Hospital.What began as a small fundraising idea has since grown into an initiative that has helped nearly 1,000 children with medical care, school supplies and everyday necessities.Teen’s cookie fundraiser grows into $66,000 nonprofitAccording to St. Jude, Kamath initially began raising money through cookie sales after returning from a summer trip to India, where he had spent time with his grandmother, whom he calls “anama.”During visits to Mumbai, Kamath accompanied his grandmother as she carried out charitable work in schools and hospitals. He remembers helping distribute notebooks and pencils to children and visiting the pediatric cancer ward at Tata Memorial Hospital, where he saw families who had travelled long distances seeking lifesaving treatment for their children.“That stuck with me through the years,” Kamath said.Those experiences eventually inspired him to find a way to support children in need in both India and the United States.From home kitchen to nonprofitBecause Kamath already enjoyed baking with his mother and grandmother, he decided cookies could become the foundation of his fundraising efforts.Chocolate chip and sugar cookies became his specialties. He initially approached local businesses and corporations, offering his baked goods in exchange for donations to children's causes.“I just kept reaching out to more people and local businesses and partnered with a few different people,” he said. “People really seemed to have an interest in it.”His parents, Ravish and Vijaya Kamath, helped by providing ingredients including flour, sugar, eggs and chocolate chips.“It is their way of contributing to my cause,” Vihaan said.In April 2025, he formally established Cookie for a Cause as a nonprofit, with proceeds going to charity. He created a website where customers could place orders and continued baking most of the cookies in his home kitchen.For larger orders, he has occasionally used a local pastry shop, whose owner and employees have supported his efforts and offered advice on improving his recipes.$20,000 raised in the first yearThe fundraiser quickly exceeded Kamath’s expectations.Between April and December 2025, Cookie for a Cause raised approximately $20,000.“From April 2025 to December 2025, we raised $20,000, which is phenomenal. I didn't even think we were going to get that far,” Kamath said.The nonprofit has since continued to grow. Kamath has now raised $66,331 and has set an ambitious target of $100,000 by the end of 2026.His father initially thought the project might eventually fade as his son balanced schoolwork and sports, but he soon realized that Kamath was committed to making it a long-term effort.“I didn’t know how far he would go with this,” Ravish Kamath said. “It was surprising, but he started to get on social media channels for this and then started to reach out to local businesses. It is now something considerable that he has done.”St. Jude becomes a key part of his missionKamath eventually expanded his fundraising to support children in the United States and connected with St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital.“I found St. Jude to be one of the best places to partner with and help out,” he said.He was later accepted into the St. Jude Leadership Society, a program that gives high school students an opportunity to develop leadership skills while raising funds and awareness for children treated by St. Jude.His connection with St. Jude also has roots in his experiences in India. Tata Memorial Hospital is part of the St. Jude Global Alliance, which brings together institutions around the world to improve care for children with cancer and other catastrophic diseases.Teen plans to keep nonprofit going after collegeKamath has no plans to stop baking once he graduates from high school.He wants to study business in college and has already begun building a student team that can continue Cookie for a Cause after he leaves for university.“I created a student board with sophomores and freshmen from my school who will continue this after I move,” he said. “I’ll continue it when I go to college.”His goal is to create an organization that can continue growing even when he is no longer running its day-to-day operations.“I don’t want to stop,” Kamath said, adding that he hopes younger students can eventually take over different aspects of the nonprofit “so that this keeps growing.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Brazilian architect built a UFO-shaped house in 1974 and planned to live there temporarily; almost 50 years later, he is still living inside it
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A Brazilian architect turned an unusual housing experiment into his own long-term home when he built Casa Bola in São Paulo. Eduardo Longo began const.
articles.body: A Brazilian architect turned an unusual housing experiment into his own long-term home when he built Casa Bola in São Paulo. Eduardo Longo began constructing the spherical residence in 1974, completing it in 1979 after building it largely by hand. Designed as a prototype for a different way of living, this 8-metre-wide structure challenged the straight walls and conventional layouts common in homes. More than four decades later, the futuristic sphere remains closely connected to Longo himself. In 2026, it finally opened to the public as part of the ABERTO5 exhibition.How a Brazilian architect’s idea of a UFO-shaped house became a realityCasa Bola emerged from Longo’s interest in changing the way people could live. Rather than designing another conventional house, he explored the possibility of spherical housing that could work as a flexible living unit. Architecture Hunter reports the project as a prototype for a lighter and more adaptable form of living, with the potential for such units to be replicated or even transported.The idea was unique for 1970s São Paulo. The sphere was not chosen simply because it looked futuristic. According to Domus, Longo considered the shape an efficient way of enclosing space while using less material. His larger vision involved prefabricated spherical homes that could be placed within a new kind of urban environment.That ambition eventually produced a single full-scale example. Longo built Casa Bola between 1974-1979 above his own office and residence in the Itaim Bibi district. According to ArchDaily, the completed structure has an 8-metre diameter and remains suspended above the rooftop slab of the property.The 5-year construction created a fascinating interior of the UFO-houseThe construction process was just as unconventional as the finished shape. ArchDaily reports that Longo built the house by hand, forming ferrocement over a complicated framework of recycled steel tubes. Instead of treating the walls, furniture and fittings as separate elements, he incorporated them into the continuous structure.Inside, the absence of conventional corners changes how the space is used. Architecture Hunter reports that the curved geometry creates a continuous environment in which movement becomes part of the experience of living. The house does not divide space in quite the same way as a conventional rectangular home.ABERTO describes the interior as being organised through continuous routes, changes in level and different relationships between the body and the surrounding space. That arrangement makes the building more than a unique exterior. Its spherical form influences everyday movement and the way its rooms connect with one another. The result was a home that looked more like a futuristic object than an ordinary residence.Longo turned his futuristic house prototype into a lifelong homeLongo’s experiment did not develop into the widespread system of spherical housing he had envisioned. Instead, Casa Bola remained a single prototype in São Paulo. According to Domus, Longo lived in it with his family for decades, turning the experimental structure into a genuine everyday home.That long period of occupation gives Casa Bola a different significance from an architectural model or an unbuilt concept. It was not simply an idea presented on paper. Longo tested his ideas by living inside the result.The house also remained surprisingly discreet despite its striking appearance. ArchDaily describes it as almost imperceptible within São Paulo’s urban landscape, even though its unusual form sets it apart from the surrounding buildings.For years, therefore, Casa Bola was primarily a private residence not a public architectural attraction. Its significance was known within architectural circles, while most people could not simply walk inside and experience its spaces.ABERTO5 brought the private sphere into public viewIn 2026, ABERTO5 opened Casa Bola to visitors for the first time. The official ABERTO website says the fifth edition ran from 8 March to 31 May 2026 and occupied the house as part of an exhibition combining art, architecture and design.Around 60 works by more than 50 Brazilian and international artists were presented across roughly 1,000 square metres connected with the exhibition. Many of the works were created specifically for the occasion and developed in response to Casa Bola’s experimental character.The exhibition also included material documenting Longo’s wider career, including drawings, photographs, models and other projects spanning decades. This gave visitors an opportunity to see the spherical house not as an isolated curiosity, but as part of the architect’s broader thinking about architecture.The building itself became an important part of the exhibition. Instead of serving merely as a neutral backdrop, its curves, circulation and compact spaces shaped how the artworks were experienced.A 1970s vision still stands in São PauloCasa Bola remains a rare example of an architectural experiment that became an enduring home. Longo’s original ideas about spherical, flexible housing did not transform the way cities were built, but the prototype survived and continued to be inhabited.Its opening through ABERTO5 offered a rare chance to examine those ideas from inside. As reported by ABERTO, the building represents a manifesto-like work of Brazilian architecture that had remained a discreet presence in São Paulo.For Longo, however, Casa Bola was never simply a historical object. It became part of his everyday life. Built during a period when architects were imagining radically different futures for housing, the sphere has now outlived many of the predictions surrounding it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
